content:
Think of a person walking around a room while keeping their face pointed toward the middle. If they walk one full lap and turn once, then after the lap the same side of their face is again facing the middle.

The Moon does the same thing around Earth. It spins once for every trip around Earth, so the side that faces Earth stays facing Earth. Earth’s gravity has pulled on the Moon for a very long time—like a slow tug on its “tides”—and that tug slowed the Moon’s spin until it matched its orbit. That’s called tidal locking.

So the Moon is not “stuck” in one place; it moves around Earth. But it keeps pace with its spin, which is why we always see the same face—the near side—from Earth.
